output.headline: Healey weighs bigger energy discount for low-income households in budget
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.

The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.

Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.

Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.

If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.

Related: Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budget

The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.

He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.

Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.

But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.

As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.

The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.

Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.

Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.

Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.

She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?

“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”

Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.

Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.

Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.

“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”

A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.

Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.

An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.

The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.

Related: Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%

Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”

He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”

Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.

“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: John Healey is working on a package of more than £1bn to help with energy bills, likely including a bigger discount for benefit claimants, as forecasts show January bills could rise by up to £442.
output.progress: Energy department officials are also working on longer-term reforms that could change how much companies charge poorer or low-energy-use households after the budget.

output.headline: Four of five Green MPs oppose party's 'Zionism is racism' vote
output.bodyHtml:
Four of the Green party's five MPs opposed the policy treating Zionism as a form of racism, before party members voted to adopt it by 1,022 votes to 813 at the party's conference in Brighton on Sunday.

Zack Polanski, who left the Green conference early on Friday to campaign, stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion. In a statement on Monday night, after the European Greens and German Greens had distanced themselves from the policy, Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state 'are and must always be completely distinct'. He said he remained proud of the party's stance on Palestinian rights.

The policy, which Green members adopted as binding, says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.

Senior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in future after they adopted a policy treating Zionism as a form of racism.

One Labour minister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement.

After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move 'shameful', saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitism under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn.

While Phillipson's statement was backed by her fellow ministers, there was debate as to whether Labour should go further and formally rule out any ties with the Greens, for example if a future general election delivered a hung parliament.

A source linked to the Jewish Labour Movement said Labour should 'absolutely' rule out governing with the Greens, arguing the policy raised serious questions about whether its treatment of Jewish members could breach equality law.

There is also pressure within the Liberal Democrats for them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski's party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London.

The Lib Dems and Greens already govern together in Southwark after May's local elections, with the Greens as the senior partner.

Following the Zionism motion, both Southwark parties released a 'joint administration statement against antisemitism'. Without mentioning the new Green policy, it said they would 'continue to work with Jewish community organisations to make sure they know they have a place in Southwark'.

It brought a scathing response from some senior Lib Dems. Tagging Victor Chamberlain, the Lib Dem deputy leader of Southwark, Sarah Ludford, a peer and former MEP for the party, wrote on X that she did not understand 'how you think this greenwash is an adequate response to the Greens' antisemitic "Zionism is racism" motion, from which I believe you should entirely distance yourselves'.

Another Lib Dem peer, Lynne Featherstone, who was formerly an MP, replied to a post by Chamberlain to say: 'I would ditch them. Grow a pair!'

It follows months of speculation of possible cooperation between the parties. Polanski said earlier this year that the Greens could consider an electoral pact with Labour under Andy Burnham or Angela Rayner, while ruling out one under the former prime minister Keir Starmer.

Labour views the Zionism motion, and the criticism that has followed, as a means to simplify its political argument against the Greens at a time when Polanski's party has increasingly sought to attract disillusioned Labour voters on the party's left.

A big test of this will come on Thursday, with voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Starmer's former seat from Labour.

The Greens have poured huge resources into the contest, with Polanski telling the Guardian that it is 'really on a knife-edge'. Despite the Greens' campaigning efforts, helped by their massively increased membership, Labour is considered the favourite to win.
output.standfirst: Four of the Green party's five MPs opposed the 'Zionism is racism' motion, passed 1,022 to 813, as senior Labour and Lib Dem figures debate whether to rule out cooperating with the party.
output.progress: Four of the Green party's five MPs opposed the policy, and senior Labour figures are debating whether to formally rule out any coalition.

output.headline: Foreign Press Association vows West Bank reporting will continue
output.bodyHtml:
The Foreign Press Association says journalists in the West Bank ‘will not be deterred’, after armed Israeli settlers beat an AFP photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.

Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.

Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.

Related: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family

“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.

The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.

“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.

“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”

His assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.

This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.

Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.

A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.

At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.

A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.

“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.

Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.

The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.

Related: UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians

AFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.

Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.

Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.

There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.

Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.

About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.

Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.

Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.

Agence France-Presse contributed reporting
output.standfirst: The Foreign Press Association says journalists ‘will not be deterred’, after armed settlers beat AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh with rifle butts as Israeli soldiers stood by, hospitalising him while he covered violence against olive farmers.
output.progress: AFP and the Foreign Press Association have demanded investigations into the attack and the soldiers’ failure to intervene.

output.headline: WHO finds no sign of further plague outbreak in Russia
output.bodyHtml:
The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia.

Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied.

Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals.

Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown ​symptoms of illness,” he said.

The WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” for Europe, Lindmeier said, while Russian officials were still investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death.

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia on Tuesday to be transparent about Shipilova’s death.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he wrote on X.

Sixty of Shipilova’s colleagues have been kept in quarantine at the institute where she worked since Friday while tests are carried out, according to Russian media, with similar measures imposed in five hospitals; colleagues have been sleeping on the floors and chairs, and relatives have been forbidden to see patients.

The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. It said the situation in Irkutsk was stable, with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees.

Washington has been watching developments closely. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon ⁠Russia to obviously share more information with ​the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour ‌by hour.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that the US state department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations.

Trump said on Tuesday that he was due to speak shortly with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the technician’s death.

“I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”.

Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters.

In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.

“The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.

*With Agence France-Presse
output.standfirst: The World Health Organization says the epidemic risk in Russia is low and has found no sign of further outbreak, after Darya Shipilova, a lab technician, died last week at a Siberian plague institute.
output.progress: Russian authorities have quarantined Shipilova's colleagues and reported no new cases, while WHO chief Tedros has urged Moscow to share full details.

output.headline: Nazir Afzal leads first stage of Cambridge’s review into Jason Arday’s death
output.bodyHtml:
Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, is already leading the first stage of Cambridge University’s review into the circumstances of Prof Jason Arday’s death, focusing on the support he was given immediately beforehand. But senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s wider plans to investigate his death as inadequate, and said those responsible for ‘serious failures of leadership’ should face consequences.

In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said ‘it is not yet clear’ how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.

Arday died at his home in London on 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

Related: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review

An inquest will be held to determine the cause of death.

Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.

Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a ‘thorough and transparent’ examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.

Rather than reviewing the ‘lessons learned’, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.

‘The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,’ the letter says.

The signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.

Cambridge last month announced a two-part review, with part one to be led by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.

The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be ‘a broader review of institutional processes and practice’ and only consider ‘the wider context’ of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.

Related: Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research

The group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the ‘scope and investigative character’ of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.

They wrote: ‘To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.

‘The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.

‘At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.’

The University of Cambridge was approached for its response to the letter.

Cambridge publicised Arday’s appointment at the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would ‘inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area’.

Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.
output.standfirst: Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor, is leading the first stage of Cambridge’s review into Jason Arday’s death, but more than 40 academics say the university has backed away from its promised thorough inquiry
output.progress: Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor, is leading the review’s first stage, examining the support given to Arday before his death.

context.text: Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, Deborah Prentice, has said she is committed to ensuring the review’s recommendations are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering changes.

output.headline: Rediscovered Scots film could claim cinema’s ‘first talkie’ crown
output.bodyHtml:
For almost a century, The Jazz Singer has been celebrated as the world’s first feature-length film to include synchronised dialogue (known as a “talkie”), and English as the first language of cinema. Now a chance discovery suggests that crown may belong instead to a film made in Glasgow and written in Scots, released a full year earlier.

The breakthrough was made by the historian and self-confessed “film nerd” Marc David Jacobs, who was conducting research for a book on the first wave of British sound films when he came across the story of Till the Bells Ring.

The 46-minute feature film, featuring spoken parts and synchronised sound throughout, premiered in Edinburgh in October 1926, a year before The Jazz Singer, starring Al Jolson, reached New York’s screens to widespread fanfare and took its place in the history books.

“This was the start of what we would consider modern film,” Jacobs said. “It was a completely new art form at the time, and if it had been taken up in Britain there could have been a real alternative history of cinema where the Americans didn’t take over and get such a lead on things.”

The creation of the Scottish playwright Graham Moffat, Till the Bells Ring is a domestic comedy set in Glasgow and performed by Moffat’s six-part touring company, including his wife, Margaret, and daughter Winifred, in what he called “lowland braid Scots”: a term for plain-language Scots dialect originating from central and southern Scotland.

It was billed at the time as a “super talking picture … of Victorian family life” and heralded upon its premiere as a cinematic milestone. The Edinburgh Evening News wrote in a review: “Even America has never attempted such a work … So perfect was the synchronisation between the image on screen and the broad Scots dialogue spoken by the image, that one might quite well have been listening to a legitimate stage version of the comedy.”

But Jacobs said the film was quickly forgotten about. “This fits into a larger narrative about British cinema, which has been uniquely neglected,” he said. “I think if it had been celebrated as a distinctly Scottish production, it might have survived or been discovered by now. But it’s fallen under this rubric of British cinema and there’s no real sense that British cinema history is actually worth looking at.”

There is no evidence that the film was ever screened publicly again after its week-long run in Edinburgh’s Poole’s Synod Hall, where the city’s Traverse theatre stands today. Moffat died in 1951 having never made another film.

Two of the film’s reels, comprising more than half its length, survive in the BFI National Archives in Hertfordshire among Jacobs’ discoveries, though they have never been screened since their acquisition more than 50 years ago. With this year marking the film’s centenary, Jacobs hopes that will change.

“I hope this becomes more than just a Scottish story, and that archives around the world might be able to take a look and maybe find the missing reel,” he said. “But this is a film that had its origins as a stage play and the manuscripts have survived, so you can imagine perhaps playing those surviving reels and then performing that missing part on stage.

“It would be an amazing moment to recreate this important landmark in world cinema history. But beyond that, hopefully it spurs people on to reconsider British cinema history as a whole and think: if this has been sitting around for 100 years, what else might be out there?”
output.standfirst: Till the Bells Ring, made in Glasgow and performed in Scots, is now thought to have beaten The Jazz Singer to the screen by a year, predating Al Jolson’s landmark spoken lines.

output.headline: Jaguar’s new EV marks crucial step in over £15bn UK investment plan, minister says
output.bodyHtml:
Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night, marking the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history.

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “Jaguar’s new EV is a crucial step in JLR’s plans to invest over £15bn in the UK, and another big vote of confidence in our world-class automotive industry.

“This cutting-edge new model being designed, engineered and built in Britain will support thousands of jobs across the West Midlands and North West, and builds on over £1bn of UK automotive investment secured just last month – marking another step forward in our mission to reindustrialise Britain.”

Starting at £130,000 ($172,000) and aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America, the Type 01 has no rear window and will not fit into a UK parking space.

Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director.

With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000.

Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.”

A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’”

Parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn, with the launch coming at a critical juncture as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its falling UK market share.

JLR recently announced 4,000 job cuts in an attempt to save £1.7bn over two years, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The Guardian understands Jaguar employees working on the Type 01 programme were offered voluntary redundancy along with the rest of JLR’s non-manufacturing workforce.

The car will go on sale in early 2027, with the first deliveries anticipated in the second half of the year.

“It’s really important that we put Jaguar back on a more solid financial footing,” Glover said, arguing that doubling prices was a better strategy than “to toil away as we have done for the last two decades in the volume premium space”.

Range Rover also unveiled its first fully electric model in September, with a starting price of £154,070 compared with £107,530 for its combustion engine predecessor.

Glover said Jaguar had decided to hold off launching the Type 01 in China for “a couple of years”, as waning demand in the country – a key market for luxury cars – has also hit the brand hard.

However, he added that China would eventually be “an important part of the equation … it’s very difficult for any car manufacturer to exclude the single largest car market in the world.”

PB Balaji, the JLR chief executive, has said the parent company will pivot towards North America and target more sales to millionaires and billionaires to turn its fortunes around.

Glover admitted that while the Type 01’s launch was in New York, it “absolutely” could have been in Silicon Valley instead, reflecting the type of buyer Jaguar is targeting. He recently took a prototype to the offices of Nvidia, the California-based AI company, whose boss, Jensen Huang, had a ride and “loved it”.

The car has no rear window, instead mounting a rear-facing camera where a traditional mirror would be. It produces more than 1,000 horsepower and Jaguar says it will travel up to 400 miles on a single charge.

It follows a controversial rebrand that started with an ad in late 2024 featuring stern-faced models without a car in sight. The ad prompted a backlash online and was followed by the Type 00 concept car, unveiled in “Miami pink”, which Donald Trump described as “woke” while Nigel Farage said Jaguar deserved to go bust.

Glover admitted the backlash “wasn’t always easy” but added: “The reality is we will need to attract a new audience.”

At 2 metres (6ft 5in) wide, the Type 01 will hog the British country lanes frequented by Jaguar’s old customer base, and at more than 5.2 metres in length it will not fit in a standard 4.8-metre UK parking space.

“There are long cars out there on the market,” Glover argued, adding that a Land Rover Defender with a wheel on the back is longer than the Type 01, which he claimed had the “turning circle of a Fiat 500” with its all-wheel steering. “It is incredibly manoeuvrable.”
output.standfirst: Jaguar’s £130,000 Type 01 arrives in New York as ministers hail over £15bn of UK investment and thousands of jobs, even as parent company JLR cuts 4,000 roles following a £1.9bn cyber-attack.
output.progress: Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds says the launch marks a step in over £15bn of planned UK investment and will support thousands of jobs.

context.text: JLR gave extra training to 10,500 staff on Range Rover’s electric model and tested it for the equivalent of 38 trips around the world.

output.headline: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning star of On the Waterfront, dies aged 102
output.bodyHtml:
Eva Marie Saint, whose screen career spanned six decades, from making her debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront to starring in Alfred Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest and, in one of her last screen appearances, playing Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film Superman Returns, has died aged 102. She was one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s.

A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.

Related: Eva Marie Saint – a life in pictures

Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine which started with the prophetic words: “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – it followed her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful.

Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent that On the Waterfront director Elia Kazan spotted her in The Trip to Bountiful and invited her to audition by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. Saint said she found the experience difficult, but was offered the role of Edie Doyle, Brando’s love interest, in the hardhitting drama about mob union activities; she would go on to win the Oscar for best supporting actress in 1955.

Related: Eva Marie Saint’s best films – ranked

After this meteoric success, Saint quickly began securing a wide variety of leading roles. She starred opposite Bob Hope in That Certain Feeling, played a woman married to a secret drug addict in the Fred Zinnemann-directed issue picture A Hatful of Rain and co-starred with Elizabeth Taylor in the period western Raintree County. Saint then achieved the highly coveted role opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy classic North by Northwest: secret agent Eve Kendall, “a blond who has all the answers”. She said in a TCM interview that she got her career-defining role – partly – by wearing beige and white gloves to a lunch appointment with Hitchcock.

Saint kicked off the 1960s by playing American nurse Kitty Fremont in Exodus, the hit adaptation of Leon Uris’s novel about the creation of the state of Israel, but subsequently eased up on her workload to prioritise her young family. In 1962 she appeared opposite Warren Beatty in All Fall Down as a woman infatuated with Beatty’s drifter, starred as Richard Burton’s wife in The Sandpiper in 1965 alongside Elizabeth Taylor and played a journalist who has an affair with Yves Montand’s race driver in Grand Prix in 1966.

Despite critical acclaim for her role in the 1970 infidelity drama Loving alongside George Segal, Saint’s film parts largely dried up in the 70s and 80s, with the actor instead turning to TV movies and guest appearances.

Sporadic film appearances ensued after a “comeback” in the 1986 Tom Hanks/Jackie Gleason comedy Nothing in Common; later appearances included as Sam Shepard’s mother in the Wim Wenders-directed western Don’t Come Knocking in 2005, and a year later she was cast in Superman Returns – where she was “reunited” with On the Waterfront star Brando, whose estate gave permission for 1978 footage to be used in the film after his death in 2004.

Saint worked more consistently in TV, winning a best supporting actress Emmy award for the 1990 mini-series People Like Us, adapted from Dominick Dunne’s novel. Her final onscreen role was in Winter’s Tale as the sister of the seemingly immortal Colin Farrell.

Saint married Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children; they remained together until his death in 2016.
